newsitem.title: ZAIRE: In Zaire refugees die, students storm parliament.
newsitem.headline: In Zaire refugees die, students storm parliament.

text.p: Rwandan refugees who fled fighting are dying of thirst in the mountains of east Zaire, U.N. officials said, and the first Zaireans arrived on Thursday with swollen feet more than 500 km (300 miles) from the war zone.

In the Zairean capital Kinshasa, thousands of students calling for the resignation of part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo took over parliament. Witnesses said unarmed gendarmes and troops were also in the building.
The first 50 Zairean men and women trekked into the Zairean city of Kisangani, sick, with swollen feet and their belongings gone, and said hundreds more were behind them, an aid worker said.

"We have no means of taking care of them -- no food, no medicine. It's a catastrophe," Claude Olenga, administrator of the church charity CARITAS, told Reuters in Kisangani, the last major Zairean outpost before a vast stretch of hills and jungle.
Olenga said the 50 said they set off from Bukavu, some 530 km (330 miles) southeast of Kisangani and one of three major east Zaire towns seized by Tutsi rebels in three weeks of fighting.
Rwandan refugees arriving in the Rwandan town of Gisenyi bordering on the Zairean city of Goma told U.N. officials of many deaths in the waterless, volcanic mountains north of Lake Kivu.

"They said they saw people dying all around them due to lack of water on the escarpment above Kahindo and Katale camps. One man was sucking water out of tree roots," said Peter Kessler, Nairobi spokesman of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees.
The east Zaire conflict has thrown Kinshasa into political turmoil.
Carrying coffins of two students killed in earlier protests, thousands of students calling for the resignation of Kengo seized the parliament building in Kinshasa. Security forces did not intervene.

Students in the capital, denouncing government handling of the three-week Tutsi rebellion in the east, have staged a series of protests this week and denounced Rwanda, which has sent in some troops of its Tutsi-dominated government army to back the rebels.
Riled by a lack of support for its plans with France to send in a multinational force, Spain accused the international community of neglecting problems in central Africa for years.
"(There has been) great carelessness by the world community," said Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes, adding the international community had only addressed the symptoms of trouble since 1994.

A foreign ministry spokesman in Madrid said on Wednesday Spain and France wanted to send a force of at least 5,000 soldiers to Zaire but would not go ahead unless the United States and United Nations backed it.
European Union aid ministers met in Brussels on Thursday to try to define a joint approach to the deepening tragedy, but there was a sharp divergence of views among aid organisations.
U.N. refugee chief Sadaka Ogata, in Brussels for the EU meeting, said the international community should send a "neutral force" empowered to arrest and disarm militias and other groups.
"I would like to see them empowered to do that, that should be one of their functions if such a force goes in," Ogata said.
Eastern Zaire is awash with arms, as a U.N. report made clear this week, and disarming everyone would be a tall order.
"Military intervention is not the answer in Zaire. It will take too long and, even if agreed, may well compound the problems in the region," the Save the Children Fund said.
Aid agencies have been ringing alarm bells about the 1.2 million refugees in eastern Zaire for weeks, but efforts to help have so far faded before the sheer complexities of the task.
Half the refugees are under the age of 16 and the part of east Zaire where they are dying is no longer in government hands.
It is held by an extraordinary medley of armies and militias acting out tribal and political rivalries, fuelled by land hunger, which threaten to tear Zaire apart.
Most of the refugees are Rwandan Hutus who fled into Zaire after the Hutu genocide of up to one million Tutsis and other victims in Rwanda in 1994.
The rebels who captured much of eastern Zaire in a two-week lightning offensive include Tutsis, the Hutus' foes.

Many refugees fear that if they return to their countries of origin, Rwanda and Burundi, they will be slaughtered by Tutsi-led armies. Only about 2,000 Rwandan refugees have returned to Rwanda in recent weeks, U.N. officials say.
More than 20,000 Zairean refugees have fled the mayhem.
Wendy Driscoll, a spokeswoman for CARE International in Nairobi, had reports of a 14 percent severe malnutrition rate among refugee children under five arriving in Tanzania.
On Wednesday Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko gave his support for an international intervention force for the east.
Mobutu, in France after treatment in Switzerland for cancer, has warmed to the French plan for an intervention force, hoping perhaps it might be a way to reassert his control in the east.
U.N. Special Envoy Raymond Chretien, who met Mobutu on Wednesday, was due in Nairobi on Thursday before Rwanda on Friday.
